title: what the Rig Veda is
hook: a friend's replies go cold, and nobody will say why. In one Rig Veda hymn, the poet Vasishtha asks Varuna straight out: what did I do?

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the Rig Veda is: many gods, and a verse saying the wise call the one by many names. Did someone call you by a name only they use? Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven.

The messages used to come every day. Jokes, photos, long voice notes. Now a friend answers in one word, or not at all. Something happened, but what? You scroll back through the chat looking for the moment it changed. You ask a mutual friend, carefully. They shrug: yeah, seems like they're upset with you. That's all anyone will say. So there's only one honest move left, and it's the hardest one: go to the friend and ask, what did I do? The Rig Veda has a hymn where a poet makes exactly that move, and the one he asks is a god.
screen: `THE MESSAGES GO QUIET.` → `SEEMS LIKE THEY'RE UPSET.` → `WHAT DID I DO?`

segments.voice: The god is Varuna. In the hymns, Varuna keeps rita, the right order of things, and he sees what people do. The poet is Vasishtha, a seer tradition remembers as the voice of these hymns. And something has gone wrong between them. In paraphrase, Vasishtha says: I ask about this wrong, Varuna, wanting to understand. I go to the wise to ask. The sages all tell me the same thing: Varuna is angry with you. So he turns to Varuna himself. What was my great offense, he asks, that you would strike the friend who sings your praise? Tell me, and I'll come to you quickly, bowing, free of it. Then he asks to be released from the wrongs of his fathers, and from the ones he did himself. And then comes a startling line. It wasn't my own will, Varuna, he says. It was drink, anger, the dice, thoughtlessness. The older one leads the younger astray. Even sleep doesn't keep wrongdoing away. Some readers hear an excuse in that. Others hear a man naming his weak spots out loud: strong drink, a temper, gambling, not thinking. Either way, he doesn't hide them. He brings them to the one he has wronged, and asks to be set right.
screen: `VARUNA SEES WHAT PEOPLE DO.` · `THE SAGES SAY: HE'S ANGRY.` · `WHAT WAS MY OFFENSE?` · `DRINK, ANGER, DICE, CARELESSNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask Vasishtha's question, gently. Sit, and let the breath slow down. Let one strained relationship come to mind, at home, at work, anywhere. Don't argue your side. Just ask, quietly: what part of this might be mine? See what comes up. If something does, name it plainly, the way Vasishtha named drink and anger and dice. No punishment. Just honesty. Then let the breath carry it for a while. If you pray, you can bring that honesty to God in your own words. The bell holds the time.
What the Rig Veda is. Not only hymns of praise, but a seer asking Varuna what he did wrong, and naming his own weak spots out loud. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what the Rig Veda is. Today, if something feels off with someone, try Vasishtha's way: skip the go-betweens and ask, kindly, what happened? Day one thousand two hundred forty-seven.

screen: `DAY 1247 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT THE RIG VEDA IS.`

howItsDone: Hymns to Varuna are read in Hindu tradition as prayers for release from wrongdoing, and the theme of asking forgiveness for faults, known and unknown, appears in prayers and rites of atonement.

match.prompt: Vasishtha and Varuna — tap the pairs.

myth: the Rig Veda contains only praise of the gods
in one hymn, Vasishtha asks Varuna what wrong he did, and asks to be released from it.
Vasishtha names his weak spots out loud
drink, anger, the dice, thoughtlessness: he says these led him astray.
Vasishtha blames the sages for Varuna's anger
the sages only tell him Varuna is angry. he goes to Varuna himself to ask why.

fork.setup: you're Vasishtha. the wise all tell you the same thing: Varuna is angry with you. what do you do?
options: stay away from Varuna until it blows over.
go to Varuna and ask what you did.
find a different god to praise.
fork.reveal: he asks Varuna directly: what was my offense? tell me, and I'll come to you quickly, bowing.

original.note: Sanskrit: Varuna, the Vedic god who keeps rita, the right order, and sees what people do.

trapdoor: what you thought: Vedic hymns are all praise and ritual.
what it means: a seer asks a god what he did wrong, and names drink, anger, dice and thoughtlessness.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 7.86, Vasishtha's hymn to Varuna, where the older leads the younger astray and even sleep does not keep wrongdoing away.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

sources.ref: Rig Veda 7.86.3–6 (I ask, wishing to know; the sages say Varuna is angry; what was the chief offense; release us from the wrongs of our fathers and our own; it was not our own will: drink, anger, dice, thoughtlessness; the older leads the younger astray; even sleep does not ward off wrong)
